blocks.text: Why Replicate a Production Database Locally?

content: I personally faced a situation where a bug was happening
. No matter how hard I tried, I just couldn’t reproduce it locally.
Why? Because of:

items: A specific data structure causing unexpected behavior
A rare edge case hidden in real user data
An unforeseen scenario I never anticipated

content: Without the exact data, debugging became almost impossible. At the same time, experimenting directly on production is dangerous.
So the safest solution was to create a local replica and debug freely. Once you have a local copy, you can:

items: Simulate edge cases and break things ( without consequences )

blocks.text: 2. Create a Docker Volume for MongoDB Data

content: To make sure your MongoDB data persists even if the container stops or restarts, we’ll create a dedicated Docker volume.
Run the following command in your terminal:
This volume will be used to store MongoDB data persistently. Once created, Docker will automatically manage this volume for us.
Now, let’s start a MongoDB container and connect it with:

items: A persistent Docker volume (for database data)
A bind mount (for accessing the dump files)

content: Run the following command in your terminal:

blocks.code:
docker run -d \
  --name mongo_container \
  -p 27017:27017 \
  -v mongo_vol:/data/db \
  -v /home/john/work/dump/database_name:/dump \
  -e MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_USERNAME=admin \
  -e MONGO_INITDB_ROOT_PASSWORD=admin \
  -e MONGO_INITDB_DATABASE=<db_name> \
  mongo

content: Make sure to replace /home/john/work/dump/db_name with the actual path to your dump directory and <db_name>with the name of the database you want to create.
Explanation

items: -d → Runs the container in detached mode (in the background)
--name mongo_container → Assigns a name to the container
-p 27017:27017 → Maps container port 27017 to your local machine
-v mongo_vol:/data/db → Mounts the persistent volume for MongoDB data
-v /home/john/work/dump/d:/dump → Makes the dump folder available inside the container

content: Once this command runs successfully, your MongoDB container will be up and running with persistent storage and access to your dump files.
Now that the container is running and the dump folder is mounted, it’s time to restore the data into MongoDB.
Since the dump folder is flat (all .bson files are in a single directory), we need to explicitly specify the target database name.
Run the following command:

blocks.code:
docker exec -it mongo_container \
  mongorestore \
  --username admin \
  --password admin \
  --authenticationDatabase admin \
  --db <db_name> \
  /dump

content: Make sure <db_name> matches the value you provided in MONGO_INITDB_DATABASE when creating the container.

items: docker exec -it mongo_container → Runs a command inside the running container
mongorestore → Restores data from the dump files
--db <db_name> → Target database for restoration (same as MONGO_INITDB_DATABASE)
/dump → Path inside the container where the dump is mounted

content: After this command gets executed, all collections (such as users, students, payments, etc.) will be restored into your local database.
Now that the database container is up and running, you can connect to your local database using the following connection string:
Replace <db_name> with the name of your specific database.
This connection string allows you to access your database with the admin credentials and ensures the connection is properly authenticated.
With the connection verified, you’re all set! You now have a fully functional replica of your production database running locally, ready for testing, debugging, and experimentation.
Happy coding!
